claims.text: Variations in constituent atomic size produce local lattice distortion in multi-component concentrated alloys.
The degree of local lattice distortion governs alloy strength and deformation behavior.
Local lattice distortion impedes dislocation motion.
At otherwise similar phase constitution and microstructure, an alloy with greater atomic-size mismatch will have higher yield strength than a lower-mismatch baseline.
At otherwise similar phase constitution and microstructure, greater atomic-size mismatch will alter ductility relative to the baseline.
The proposed comparison uses single-phase, homogenized FCC alloys with controlled, equiaxed grain structures.
Changing composition to introduce elements with substantially different atomic radii will increase atomic-size mismatch and lattice distortion.
Atomic-size mismatch creates local lattice strain fields.
Lattice distortions increase the critical resolved shear stress required for plastic deformation.
Lattice distortions slow dislocation mobility and thereby enhance yield strength.
Greater atomic-size mismatch will modify the strain-hardening response relative to the lower-mismatch baseline.
The proposed mechanism should apply to single-phase concentrated alloys under room-temperature tensile loading.
The proposed mechanism may cease to dominate when additional phases form or under extreme temperature or strain-rate conditions.
Chemical ordering, short-range clustering, and grain-boundary effects may independently affect strength and deformation behavior.
X-ray diffraction peak broadening or transmission electron microscopy can be used to assess atomic-scale lattice distortion.

Failure of the higher-mismatch alloy to show a statistically significant yield-strength increase and corresponding strain-hardening changes, after controlling other microstructural differences, would falsify lattice distortion as the dominant mechanism.
